records.title: Record Coral Sea heat in January to March 2024, the warmest in 400 years
records.description: A peer-reviewed reconstruction found that the January to March 2024 sea-surface temperature in the Coral Sea was the warmest in the 1618 to 2024 record, about 1.73 C above the 1618 to 1899 average. The Bureau of Meteorology reported record-high monthly sea-surface temperatures across the Coral Sea in January and April 2024 and Australian-region waters at their warmest annual average on record. The heat drove the fifth mass bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef in the past ten years.

location.name: Coral Sea and Great Barrier Reef
location.detail: Coral Sea off Queensland, Australia, including the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park

records.layer_rationale: Record sea-surface heat is a physical climate extreme measured in the water column of the Coral Sea.

notes.harm: The Bureau of Meteorology's State of the Climate 2024 lists 2024 as the fifth mass coral bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef in ten years and says accumulated thermal stress in 2024 was higher than in 2016 (ref 3); AIMS surveys reported the largest single-year coral cover declines on record in the north and south (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources documents a closure, restriction or lost income tied to the 2024 heat itself, so no disruption is scored.
notes.scale: The warmest-in-400-years finding covers the Coral Sea region off Queensland rather than a single reef, so it is scored at the regional-sea level (ref 1).
notes.duration: The reconstructed extreme covers the January to March 2024 window and the Bureau reports record monthly values in January and April, a few months in total (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Bureau of Meteorology issued the record as a formal Annual Climate Statement on 6 February 2025 (ref 2) and the finding was published in Nature (ref 1), but no enforcement or emergency action is cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: January to March 2024 Coral Sea heat extreme was the warmest in 400 years, about 1.73 C above the 1618 to 1899 reconstructed average (ref 1).

signals: The Great Barrier Reef underpins reef tourism and fisheries, but the cited sources do not quantify economic losses from the 2024 heat (refs 3, 4).

trend.note: The study reports Coral Sea warming of about 0.09 C per decade over 1900 to 2024 and 0.12 C per decade over 1960 to 2024 (ref 1).

records.title: Second consecutive marine heatwave on the Great Barrier Reef in summer 2024-25
records.description: The Reef Authority, AIMS and CSIRO reported that prolonged above-average water temperatures (marine heatwaves) in December 2024 to March 2025 caused regional coral bleaching in the Far Northern and Northern regions, the sixth mass bleaching event since 2016. Heat stress in the Southern region did not reach levels that warranted aerial bleaching surveys. AAP later reported that Australia's oceans had their warmest 12 months on record in 2024-25.

notes.livelihoods: The snapshot and news coverage cited do not document tourism closures, fishery restrictions or lost income, so none is scored.
notes.scale: Bleaching spanned two of the four Marine Park management regions, a regional-sea scale rather than one reef (ref 1).
notes.duration: The event followed the 2023-24 mass bleaching, making the Reef's second back-to-back event, with heat stress accumulating from December 2024 to March 2025 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Reef Authority, AIMS and CSIRO issued a formal end-of-summer Reef Snapshot classifying it as the sixth mass bleaching event since 2016 (ref 1), but no enforcement or emergency declaration is cited.

records.title: King tide breaches Saibai Island sea walls and floods homes in February 2026
records.description: AAP reported that king tides in early February 2026 pushed water on Saibai Island in the Torres Strait about 3.7 metres above average, breaching sea walls, flooding houses and roads and covering the cemetery. Residents said the flooding was more severe than the previous year, and that salt water is seeping into soil and making food harder to grow. The Bureau of Meteorology reports that sea level rise to the north of Australia has been significantly higher than the global average since 1993.

records.title: Federal Court rejects Torres Strait Islanders' sea-level climate claim; appeal listed for July 2026
records.description: On 15 July 2025 the Federal Court of Australia held that the Commonwealth owes Torres Strait Islanders no duty of care over climate change, in Pabai v Commonwealth (No 2) [2025] FCA 796, while accepting that the islanders have suffered and will continue to suffer from sea level rise and extreme events. The applicants' case rested on projected marine inundation and erosion of low-lying islands such as Saibai and Boigu. The applicants appealed, and the Full Federal Court was listed to hear the appeal in Melbourne over four days from 28 July 2026.

notes.harm: Justice Wigney accepted that Torres Strait Islanders have suffered and will continue to suffer from sea level rise and extreme events if greater action is not taken (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The claim cited coastal erosion, flooding, freshwater contamination and decline in traditional food sources, and the court declined to recognise loss of fulfilment of Ailan Kastom as compensable (ref 1).
notes.scale: The class action is brought for Torres Strait Islanders across the Zenadth Kes island group, a regional rather than single-site claim (ref 1).
notes.duration: The class action was commenced in March 2022, judgment was given in July 2025 and the appeal was listed for hearing from 28 July 2026, so the dispute spans several years (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A Federal Court judgment of 15 July 2025 is a court ruling, and the applicants filed an appeal to the Full Federal Court (refs 1, 3).

signals: The applicants' alternative case sought predictable funding for seawalls against marine inundation and erosion, which the court also rejected as core government policy (ref 1).

records.title: Walande community in South Malaita relocated to the mainland after king tides; seawall failing
records.description: Human Rights Watch reported in March 2025 that the roughly 800 people of Walande, South Malaita, Solomon Islands, moved from an artificial island to the mainland after repeated cyclone and king tide damage, largely at their own expense. Seawater now breaches the 2021 seawall at the new site and is destroying swamp taro land, and some residents are considering moving again. The government adopted Planned Relocation Guidelines in 2022 but has not fully operationalised them.

records.title: Cyclone Alfred swell strips beaches and dunes along South East Queensland in March 2025
records.description: The Bureau of Meteorology reported that Severe Tropical Cyclone Alfred, a long-lived Coral Sea system, produced large swell that caused significant coastal erosion along south-east Queensland and north-eastern New South Wales, with an estimated millions of cubic metres of sand scoured and dune escarpments up to 6 metres high. A coastal scientist reported storm surge of up to 0.5 metres above the high tide mark on the Gold Coast, which exposed a buried seawall. Much of the sand sits on offshore sandbars and dunes may take years to recover. Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred eroded about 6 million cubic metres of sand from Gold Coast beaches in March 2025, leaving some sand cliffs about 6 metres high; the mayor said 80% of the beach had gone into the ocean. The council used offshore dredging and dune sand to rebuild beaches. Queensland and the Australian Government later funded a $74 million environmental recovery program that includes beach replenishment.

records.title: Mass coral bleaching strikes the Great Barrier Reef in 2024 and again in 2025
records.description: Aerial surveys in March 2024 confirmed a mass bleaching event, the fifth in eight years, across more than 300 reefs covering about two-thirds of the World Heritage Area. AIMS later reported that the 2024 event had the largest spatial footprint of any bleaching on record, and a smaller event followed in 2025 with medium to high bleaching on 41% of surveyed inshore and mid-shelf reefs in the north and centre. Some reefs have since recovered, for example about 90% of bleached coral at Lady Elliot Island after Cyclone Alfred cooled the water.

notes.significance: The Reef Authority formally confirmed that a widespread mass bleaching event was unfolding (ref 1).

records.title: World Heritage Committee keeps Great Barrier Reef off the In Danger list in 2026 but sets new conditions after 2025 'utmost concern'
records.description: At its 2025 session the World Heritage Committee noted with utmost concern the Reef's continued deterioration due largely to climate change and regretted that 2025 water quality targets were missed. At its 2026 session in Busan it again did not list the property as In Danger, but asked Australia for further water quality, gillnet-phase-out, dredge-spoil and climate actions, with progress reports due in 2028 and 2029. The Queensland Government says it has delivered UNESCO's recommendations since 2022. In July 2025 the World Heritage Committee ordered a full review of Great Barrier Reef management, with a State of Conservation report due in early 2026. A draft decision released on 3 July 2026 recommends against an 'in danger' listing and credits Australia's work on water quality and other pressures, but expresses 'utmost concern' about declining coral cover after the 2024 and 2025 bleaching events. Progress reports are due in December 2028 and 2029.

notes.scale: The decisions concern the whole property, which runs along the Queensland coast, so the scale is a coastline-wide protected area rather than one reef (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The Committee has reviewed the property repeatedly (decisions 45 COM 7B.13, 46 COM 7B.62, 47 COM 7B.2 and 48 COM 7B.69) and sets reporting dates to 1 December 2029 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Two Committee decisions in 2025 and 2026 set formal requests and deadlines (1 February 2026, 1 December 2028, 1 December 2029) and the 2026 session decided not to list the property In Danger (refs 1, 2, 3, 4).

records.title: Great Nicobar transshipment port and 130 sq km forest diversion cleared by the National Green Tribunal at the Galathea Bay leatherback nesting coast
records.description: On 16 February 2026 India's National Green Tribunal dismissed the coastal-zone challenges to the Rs 80,000 crore Great Nicobar project, which includes an international container transshipment terminal at Galathea Bay, a nesting ground for giant leatherback turtles that the reports say also holds corals and mangroves. The Tribunal accepted the Zoological Survey of India's suggestion that scattered corals can be translocated and ordered full compliance with the clearance conditions. Critics say the clearance rests on deference to government reports rather than a merit review, and the case remains contested. India plans an International Container Transshipment Port at Galathea Bay on Great Nicobar Island, designed to reach 16 million TEU in its final phase. In February 2026 the National Green Tribunal's eastern zonal bench upheld the project's environmental clearance, while critics cite coral, leatherback turtle and seismic risks. A detailed project report was prepared in December 2025 and a tender was reported as likely by July 2026; this record has not confirmed that a tender was issued.

records.title: Banned antibiotic residues in Indian shrimp exports are traced mainly to Andhra Pradesh farms, with a 43 percent rejection rate in 2025

records.title: Rohingya sea crossings in 2025 were the deadliest on record in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal
records.description: UNHCR said nearly 900 Rohingya were reported missing or dead in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, the deadliest year on record, with about one in seven of an estimated 6,500 people attempting the crossing lost. In April 2026 UNHCR and IOM said about 250 people were missing after a boat that left Teknaf capsized; nine survivors were rescued near the Andaman Islands. UNHCR is a refugee agency rather than an ocean body, so this is recorded as a maritime safety issue.

records.title: Kyaukphyu deep-sea port push continues in Myanmar's Rakhine while fighting surrounds the site
records.description: China and Myanmar's military government agreed on 17 June 2026 to speed up the Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port, with a first phase of about US$1.3 billion and CITIC Consortium holding 70%. Reports from Burma News International and Development Media Group say fighting between junta forces and the Arakan Army continues in Kyaukphyu Township, including near a naval base and a gas storage facility. These are mostly local outlets and the Arakan Army's and junta's claims are unverified.

records.title: Undersea fibre cable fault cuts Nancowry and Great Nicobar off from the network in September 2025
records.description: A fault on the Car Nicobar to Kamorta segment of the Chennai to Andaman and Nicobar Islands (CANI) submarine cable, about 1.06 km from the Car Nicobar beach manhole, began on 20 September 2025 and cut Nancowry and Great Nicobar to limited satellite bandwidth. The repair ship ASEAN Restorer was reported heading from Chennai to Car Nicobar on 17 October 2025, with services not yet restored. The cause was not stated.
